title: Room-temperature short-wave-infrared photon-counting cameras

concept.text: The proposed innovation is a room-temperature camera that detects individual short-wave-infrared (SWIR) photons across a large array of independently operating pixels. Each pixel would register faint light and measure photon arrival times, enabling both intensity imaging and time-of-flight depth measurements. The central breakthrough would be the simultaneous combination of high detection efficiency, low false-count rates, precise timing and large pixel count in a CMOS-compatible focal plane. Room-temperature SWIR photon detection and scanned depth imaging have already been demonstrated; the supplied evidence does not demonstrate this complete camera.

The material challenge arises because silicon has negligible optical absorption beyond approximately 1 µm. Germanium–silicon devices provide a route to detecting longer wavelengths, including the proposed operating points near 1310 or 1550 nm. In a single-photon avalanche diode, or SPAD, an absorbed photon can trigger an electrical avalanche large enough to register. The same sensitivity makes unwanted avalanches, trapped-charge effects and interactions between pixels consequential. CMOS compatibility offers a manufacturing route, but it does not by itself establish integration with CMOS readout circuitry or a working imaging array.

significance.text: A camera achieving these capabilities together would remove detector cryogenics from sensitive SWIR photon-counting imaging. The supplied manuscript describes typical superconducting nanowire detectors as operating at a few kelvin, while silicon SPADs had already entered consumer electronics as proximity sensors and near-infrared three-dimensional imagers. Extending similarly accessible photon counting into SWIR could substantially broaden where very faint light and photon arrival times can be measured. This is a conditional extension of an established imaging capability; the supplied sources do not establish matched performance between the proposed camera and a particular superconducting camera.

Lidar is a directly motivated application: the 2024 GeSi work demonstrated scanned depth imaging and discussed improved laser eye safety as a reason to pursue SWIR detection. A large focal plane could collect spatial information across many pixels without relying on the same single-detector scanning arrangement. Practical advantages would still depend on illumination, optics, background light, readout bandwidth, power consumption, fabrication yield and cost. Operating in SWIR alone does not establish that a complete lidar system meets an eye-safety requirement.

A further possibility is room-temperature detection within quantum-photonic circuits, provided the detectors can be coupled efficiently to waveguides and integrated with the required electronics. Removing detector cooling would not remove cooling required by other components. In particular, the supplied review of the cited 2025 quantum-dot source experiment identifies a cryostat housing the source itself. That experiment therefore cannot establish that improved detectors alone would make the complete quantum-photonic system operate without cryogenics.

Conditional application synthesis: telecommunications-band measurements and biomedical imaging are possible downstream uses, but their benefits would need application-specific demonstrations. The supplied review does not establish the earlier claim of deeper biomedical penetration, and detector sensitivity alone does not determine imaging depth, resolution or tissue contrast. Likewise, a useful camera would not automatically make photon counting routine across every SWIR application.

missing_breakthrough.text: The remaining capability is camera-scale performance achieved simultaneously at room temperature. Na and colleagues characterized earlier germanium-based SPADs as suffering high dark-count rates, low single-photon detection probability, or both, with useful performance generally requiring temperatures below 200 K. Their 2024 room-temperature GeSi demonstration advances beyond that historical limitation, but its reported efficiency, noise and scanned imaging do not establish a high-efficiency, low-noise focal plane. The engineering task is to improve these properties together rather than demonstrate room-temperature SWIR detection for the first time.

Dark counts are avalanches registered without the intended photon signal; afterpulsing produces additional counts associated with earlier avalanches. Both can obscure faint signals or distort timing statistics. Reducing these effects while retaining efficient photon absorption, reliable avalanche triggering and rapid recovery is a coupled device problem. A dark-count density must also be translated into counts per actual pixel and exposure: the density alone cannot establish suitability for seconds-long imaging.

The accepted manuscript identifies concrete development directions: scaling the device geometry toward imaging pixels with pitches below 10 µm, reducing contact resistance and parasitic capacitance, and integrating with CMOS circuitry through wafer-level bonding. At array scale, these developments must support usable optical fill factor, efficient coupling, sufficiently uniform pixel behavior and practical timing/readout electronics. Compatibility of the detector fabrication process with CMOS is an enabling condition, not evidence that these integration steps have already been completed.

Engineering synthesis: the camera must also control optical and electrical crosstalk, preserve low noise as many pixels operate concurrently, and manage the data and heat generated by sustained counting. High operating yield matters because a few excellent devices do not establish a useful focal plane. These system requirements connect detector materials and avalanche design to semiconductor manufacturing and camera architecture.

current_state.text: Na and colleagues reported a room-temperature, CMOS-compatible GeSi SPAD in Nature, published online on 21 February 2024 and appearing in volume 627, pages 295–300. The abstract reports a dark-count density of 19 kHz µm⁻², a single-photon detection probability of 12 percent at 1310 nm, timing jitter of 188 ps, a dead time of approximately 90 ns and afterpulsing below 1 percent. These are reported device results, not specifications demonstrated across a large focal plane. The supplied review retains the inverse-area dark-count unit consistently given in the Nature abstract and manuscript; a malformed unit on the arXiv landing page should not replace it.

The timing result requires an illumination qualification. According to the supplied review of the accepted manuscript, device-characterization measurements used a mean of 10 incident photons per pulse; jitter ranged from 115 to 207 ps over excess biases from 0.5 to 2.5 V under that condition. The abstract's 188 ps figure therefore should not be treated as an unqualified timing result under single-photon illumination. In the depth-imaging experiment, the manuscript reports approximately 294 ps after accounting for background dark counts and an approximately 99 ps contribution from the counter system. These different measurement conditions matter when comparing timing performance.

The work also demonstrated proof-of-concept depth imaging using galvo-mirror scanning with a detector. This establishes room-temperature SWIR photon-counting imaging in that experimental configuration, while leaving a focal plane of independently operating pixels undemonstrated by this work. The authors' statement that only silicon SPADs had achieved mainstream consumer-electronics success was a historical assessment, qualified in the Nature abstract as being to their knowledge at publication. It is not a complete market assessment for November 2026.

The retained Nature article provides a subscription preview rather than the full main article. However, the supplied review includes the full accepted-manuscript text available through arXiv, with methods and results that support the scanning and timing qualifications above. This manuscript corresponds to the published Nature work; it is not a separate unreviewed demonstration. Its availability supersedes the earlier research note's abstract-only limitation for those reviewed details.

For the related 2025 quantum-dot source experiment, the reviewed main-article preview reports overall source-system efficiency of 0.712(18). That quantity is not detector efficiency and does not verify the earlier claim of a superconducting detector with 79 percent efficiency. The reviewed supplementary text establishes source cryogenic operation. Another supplied supplementary PDF had essentially no extractable text, and its figures were not inspected in the review, so it cannot resolve the detector-efficiency claim here. The missing verification does not establish that the claimed detector figure is false.

Evidence boundary: the supplied record contains no completed freshness assessment establishing the field's status on 1 November 2026. It supports the dated 2024 demonstration and shows that this demonstration falls short of the proposed camera, but it cannot establish whether subsequent work has achieved the complete capability.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: operate a CMOS-compatible focal plane containing at least 10⁵ independently functioning pixels at room temperature, with single-photon detection efficiency above 50 percent near a declared operating wavelength of 1310 or 1550 nm and timing jitter below 100 ps under single-photon illumination. The demonstration should combine these properties in the same camera and operating configuration. These numbers are proposed engineering targets, not a published specification or an established benchmark for parity with superconducting cameras.
completion_criteria.label: Room-temperature ≥10⁵-pixel CMOS-compatible camera exceeds 50% efficiency with sub-100-ps jitter

completion_criteria.text: Proposed noise and rate protocol: replace the qualitative goals of seconds-long exposures and megahertz pixel rates with explicit acceptance conditions before testing. Specify per-pixel dark-count limits, exposure duration, signal and background levels, required signal-to-noise ratio, allowable afterpulsing, dead time and sustained usable count rate. Distinguish a brief peak response from continuous operation, and state whether megahertz operation is supported per active pixel, across the complete array, or only within a constrained aggregate data rate.
completion_criteria.label: Define explicit noise and sustained-rate acceptance conditions before testing

completion_criteria.text: Proposed measurement protocol: report end-to-end detection efficiency with fill factor and optical coupling losses identified, alongside any intrinsic device efficiency. Measure timing with a documented photon-number distribution and instrument-response treatment. Report pixel-to-pixel distributions, defective-pixel fraction, crosstalk, operating temperature, bias conditions, power and thermal behavior. Establish that the efficiency, noise and timing targets coexist rather than being drawn from different pixels, temperatures or bias settings.
completion_criteria.label: Report camera measurements establishing coexistence of efficiency, noise and timing targets

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility and practical boundary: reproduce the camera performance across multiple devices and fabrication runs, with independent confirmation where feasible, and demonstrate useful faint-light images and depth measurements under declared conditions. Long exposures and sustained counting should be tested separately where they represent different operating modes. Such finite tests would establish demonstrated breadth over specified wavelengths, temperatures, backgrounds and operating durations; they would not establish universal SWIR performance. Any claimed replacement for a superconducting camera would require a named comparator measured under comparable conditions.
completion_criteria.label: Reproduce imaging and depth performance across devices and fabrication runs

related_concepts.text: Roster-based synthesis: OPT-02, Arrays of deterministic single-photon sources above the loss threshold, supplies photons, whereas OPT-10 detects them. Efficient detection could complement source arrays, but source determinism, collection losses and detector efficiency remain separate requirements. The cited 2025 source experiment illustrates a further distinction: its source required cooling, so completing OPT-10 alone would not make that implementation fully room-temperature.

Roster-based synthesis: OPT-03, Room-temperature, electrically pumped laser grown in a silicon CMOS flow, shares the challenge of integrating optoelectronic materials with semiconductor manufacturing, but addresses light generation rather than photon counting. OPT-09, Few-femtojoule optical links inside computing packages, addresses communication energy; a photon-counting detector does not by itself establish a practical low-energy data link. OPT-01, Cascadable few-photon optical transistor, concerns optical switching and gain that can drive subsequent stages. Detection may support its measurement or control, but it does not establish cascadable optical logic.

Roster-based synthesis: OPT-05, Video-rate cellular imaging through living tissue, could benefit from sensitive detectors in an appropriate spectral band, but tissue scattering, contrast and image reconstruction remain distinct barriers. OPT-06, Practical visible far-field super-resolution optic, addresses spatial resolution in visible light; counting SWIR photons does not itself overcome a resolution limit. OPT-07, Macroscopic programmable visible optical aperture, controls an outgoing or transmitted wavefront, whereas OPT-10 records incoming light. Their pixel counts describe different physical functions and are not interchangeable measures of completion.

Roster-based synthesis: OPT-04, Laboratory-scale coherent hard X-ray source, concerns a different spectral regime and the generation of coherent radiation. OPT-08, The quantum vacuum as a laboratory nonlinear optical medium, concerns a fundamental light–matter interaction rather than semiconductor detection. Neither follows from completing OPT-10. OPT-10 remains the roster's distinct camera and detector-array innovation; these connections do not merge or replace any entry.

unresolved_issues: The supplied record does not establish whether the complete proposed camera remained undemonstrated on 1 November 2026.

Per-pixel dark-count limits, required exposure signal-to-noise ratio, allowable afterpulsing, operating yield and aggregate sustained-rate requirements remain to be selected for the proposed completion test.
No supplied comparator establishes superconducting-camera parity for the proposed combination of pixel count, efficiency, noise and timing.

The cited 2025 experiment's claimed 79 percent superconducting-detector efficiency remains unverified. The reviewed preview and supplementary text do not resolve it, and another supplementary PDF lacked usable extracted content.
Application-specific benefits for biomedical imaging and telecommunications, and efficient integration into quantum-photonic circuits, require evidence beyond the supplied detector demonstration.

brief.title: Cameras that count infrared light without deep cooling
possible: You could photograph faint scenes in short-wave infrared light, beyond silicon sensors’ useful detection range. A camera operating at room temperature would count photons, individual particles of light, and measure when they arrive.

The same camera could measure depth from the time light takes to return from objects. Many independently operating pixels would collect spatial information without scanning a lone detector across the scene.
why: Removing the detector’s deep-cooling equipment would broaden where sensitive infrared imaging could be used. It would extend photon counting and precise arrival-time measurements into a wavelength range that ordinary silicon detectors cannot cover.

sources.showed: They built a source of individual photons that crossed an efficiency threshold for computing with light.
sources.quote: This source for the first time reaches the efficiency threshold for scalable photonic quantum computing.
sources.cited_for: Efficient photon sources could complement efficient detectors in circuits that process information with light.
sources.not_established: The source itself required deep cooling, so improved detectors alone would not make this system operate at room temperature.

sources.who: Neil Na and colleagues at Artilux
sources.showed: They demonstrated a germanium–silicon photon detector at room temperature using a process compatible with standard chipmaking. They also produced depth images by scanning.
sources.quote: Three-dimensional point-cloud images are captured with direct time-of-flight technique as proof of concept.
sources.cited_for: Room-temperature infrared photon detection and scanned depth imaging have been demonstrated.
sources.not_established: The work did not demonstrate a large camera array combining high efficiency, low false counts and precise timing under single-photon illumination.

sources.who: Neil Na and colleagues at Artilux
sources.showed: An earlier version of the same work.

shown: Na and colleagues’ detector registered 12% of incoming photons at the tested infrared wavelength. Their depth images used a scanning detector. Their timing measurements used pulses containing several photons on average, so those measurements do not establish timing precision under single-photon illumination.
missing: A large array must combine efficient detection, precise timing and few false counts at room temperature.
The detectors still need integrated readout electronics that collect signals reliably while controlling heat and interference between pixels.
Useful faint-light imaging must survive false counts without incoming light and extra counts triggered by earlier detections.

milestones.label: A large camera meets efficiency and timing targets together
milestones.explanation: A room-temperature camera compatible with standard chipmaking would need at least 100,000 independent pixels, detect most incoming photons and meet the proposed single-photon timing target. This would unite the required capabilities.

milestones.label: Noise and counting-rate pass conditions are defined
milestones.explanation: Tests would need explicit limits for false counts, exposure conditions, recovery time and continuous counting rates. These would distinguish useful sustained operation from brief peak performance.

milestones.label: Measurements confirm the targets coexist across the camera
milestones.explanation: Measurements would need to account for optical losses, illumination, pixel variation, interference, power and heat in the same operating conditions. This would establish camera performance beyond selected detector results.

milestones.label: Imaging and depth results repeat across manufacturing runs
milestones.explanation: Multiple cameras from separate manufacturing runs would need to reproduce useful faint-light images and depth measurements under declared conditions. This would establish reliability and the boundaries of demonstrated performance.

uncertain: The proposed performance targets are engineering goals; they do not establish equivalence to a deeply cooled camera.
Acceptable false-count rates, usable-pixel yield and sustained counting capacity still need agreed thresholds.
Benefits for biomedical imaging, telecommunications and circuits that process light need application-specific demonstrations.

page.title: Room-temperature SWIR photon-counting focal-plane cameras
page.definition: A semiconductor camera counts individual short-wave-infrared (SWIR) photons across a two-dimensional detector array at laboratory ambient temperature. Integrated readout forms intensity images and depth maps from photon time of flight, the round-trip travel time of pulsed light.

goal.need: Silicon has negligible optical absorption beyond about 1 µm, motivating other detector materials for photon counting at 1310 and 1550 nm. Superconducting nanowire single-photon detectors typically operate at a few kelvin. Room-temperature semiconductor arrays provide SWIR photon counting without that cryogenic operating condition.

statements.quote: SWIR single-photon detectors operated at room temperature and being CMOS compatible are actively sought after.
These detectors require high quantum efficiencies, low dark count rates, fast recovery times, and capabilities for photon number resolving.
statements.context: Finding 3-6 discusses single-photon detectors and photon-counting imagers for communication and sensing.

statements.body: Engineering and Physical Sciences Research Council, Single Photons – Expanding the Spectrum programme
statements.context: The funded programme proposes scaling SWIR and mid-wave-infrared single-photon detectors into focal-plane arrays.

completion.title: A room-temperature SWIR focal plane produces photon-counted intensity images and time-of-flight depth maps.
completion.criterion: A two-dimensional semiconductor single-photon avalanche diode array, integrated with CMOS readout circuitry, produces intensity images from counted photon events and depth maps from the return times of pulsed illumination at a declared SWIR wavelength and laboratory ambient temperature. A single-photon avalanche diode converts a photon-triggered electrical avalanche into a detection event. No numerical minimum for pixel count, detection efficiency or timing precision, or maximum dark-count rate, is assigned.
completion.set_by: Atlas fallback: functional camera demonstration; no external combined numerical acceptance test was located.
completion.basis: Searches of EMVA 1288, NRC sensor-array guidance, DARPA Detect and EPSRC SPEXS found no combined numerical camera acceptance test. NRC Table 3-3 gives single-detector trigger points for quantum applications. The narrow functional test is achieved for InGaAs/InP: the paper published on 9 February 2026 reports 96 × 96 pixels at 1550 nm, with intensity and depth imaging at 10 m in 120 klux.

milestones.title: A semiconductor detector registers events triggered by individual SWIR photons.
milestones.criterion: Individual photons trigger registered detection events at a declared SWIR wavelength. Ge-on-Si: Na et al. characterized two 15 µm devices, S1 and S2, in 2024; their abstract reports 12% detection probability at 1310 nm. The reported 188 ps timing figure used a mean of 10 photons per pulse. InGaAs/InP: measurements reported in 2024 give 15% photon detection efficiency and a typical pixel dark-count rate of 87,000 s⁻¹ at room temperature and 1550 nm.
milestones.set_by: The single-photon-detector convention, explicitly defined by Na et al. in the accepted Nature manuscript; it specifies individual-photon sensitivity without a universal efficiency or noise threshold.
milestones.threshold_quote: may discern the smallest quanta of light

milestones.title: SWIR single-photon detectors operate in array format.
milestones.criterion: A fabricated semiconductor detector array retains single-photon sensitivity in its pixels. SPEXS specifies no minimum array dimensions. InGaAs/InP: the 2024 detector-array report includes breakdown-voltage statistics for 576 pixels and dark-count statistics for 144 pixels. Ge-on-Si: a CMOS-based flash lidar system using a 160 × 116 pixel array at room temperature was reported at CLEO, held from 4 May 2025 to 9 May 2025.
milestones.set_by: EPSRC SPEXS programme, grant EP/S026428/1, published project abstract; the array objective covers Ge-on-Si and III–V semiconductor detectors and has no numerical pixel-count threshold.

milestones.title: An SWIR single-photon array delivers photon data through integrated readout circuitry.
milestones.criterion: Readout circuitry is integrated with an SWIR semiconductor array and delivers single-photon data. SPEXS specifies no numerical latency or throughput threshold. InGaAs/InP: the 2026 imaging sensor uses a 110 nm CMOS bottom tier. Ge-on-Si: the ISSCC programme for 16 February 2026 lists a 400 × 300 pixel range sensor with programmable macro-pixels and integrated histogram processing; its full paper was inaccessible, so its detailed operating conditions remain unverified here.
milestones.set_by: EPSRC SPEXS programme, grant EP/S026428/1, published project abstract; integrated delivery of single-photon data is an explicit programme objective.
milestones.threshold_quote: integrate these arrayed detector technologies with read-out circuitry

not_found: No external camera acceptance test combining operating temperature, pixel count, detection efficiency, dark counts and timing precision was located.

The accessible 2026 InGaAs/InP abstract does not give a numerical detector temperature or functional-pixel yield.

results.finding: Two GeSi SPAD devices showed up to 24% single-photon detection probability at 1310 nm.
results.detail: Measurements were made at room temperature with a mean of 0.1 photons per pulse. The timing-jitter measurements used a mean of 10 photons per pulse.
results.quote:
SPDP between 5 % and 24 % can be reached for Vex between 
0.5 V and 2.5 V given <n>=0.1.

results.finding: Ge-on-Si SPAD pixel array, sample size unspecified: 33.8% photon detection efficiency at 1300 nm.
results.detail: The title reports the result under room-temperature conditions. The English abstract is unavailable, and the text does not state the number of devices measured.
results.quote: 10 µm Pitch Ge-on-Si SPAD Pixel Array with PDE of 33.8% at 1300 nm and 23.3% at 1550 nm under Room Temperature Environment

results.finding: Two InGaAs/InP single-photon detectors were characterized; one achieved 60.1% photon detection efficiency at 1550 nm.
results.detail: The 60.1% result was measured at 300 K, with a dark-count rate of 340,000 s⁻¹ and an afterpulse probability of 14.8%.
results.quote: Here we present the implementation of high-frequency gating InGaAs/InP SPD with a PDE as high as 60% at 1550 nm.

results.finding: A room-temperature SWIR flash LiDAR system uses a 160 × 116-pixel Ge-on-Si SPAD array.
results.detail: The source is a conference proceedings paper; the supplied text does not establish peer review.
results.quote: This study presents the first CMOS-based flash SWIR LiDAR system capable of room-temperature operation, featuring outstanding performance and pixel uniformity in a 160 × 116 pixel Ge-on-Si SPAD array, paving the way for commercial applications.

results.finding: A 32×32 Ge-on-Si SPAD array delivers per-pixel photon counts through a stacked 40 nm CMOS readout.
results.detail: The measured 1300 nm photon detection probability was 7% at −40°C and 2 V excess bias. During measurements, only one-quarter of the SPADs were biased above breakdown at a time.
results.quote:
The 32x32 readout circuit gives access to the count  per 
second (cps) of each individual pixel.

results.finding: Two GeSi SPADs were characterized; the reported single-photon detection probability was 12% at 1310 nm.
results.detail: Measurements were conducted at room temperature. The reported timing jitter used a mean of 10 photons per pulse.

results.finding: One 100 µm Ge-on-Si SPAD achieved 38% single-photon detection efficiency at 1310 nm.
results.detail: The measurement was made at 125 K with a gated detector and attenuated laser pulses. The source does not demonstrate room-temperature operation.
results.quote: This planar geometry has enabled a significant step-change in performance, demonstrating single-photon detection efficiency of 38% at 125 K at a wavelength of 1310 nm, and a fifty-fold improvement in noise equivalent power compared with optimised mesa geometry SPADs.

results.finding: One InGaAs/InP detector achieved over 55% single-photon detection efficiency at 1550 nm.
results.detail: The detector operated at room temperature with 1 GHz gating. Efficiency was measured using pulses averaging 0.1 photons per pulse.

The SPDE rises to over 55% at room temperature  which is the highest reported  with an
